title: Workload identity in the cluster: pods without a static secret

videos.script: The shop's order API needs to write to a storage account. The quickest way is a client secret in a Kubernetes secret. It works on the first afternoon, and it is wrong on every day after it. {{secret}} This lesson starts with why. The secret gets copied into places nobody tracks. It expires on a date somebody set a year ago, or it never does. And every pod that holds it is the same application. {{token}} Then it builds the replacement, starting with something the cluster already has. Kubernetes signs a token for every service account. You will make one with Entra ID as its audience, on kind, and read every claim in it. {{trust}} Next, the Azure side. A federated credential on a managed identity names one issuer, one subject and one audience. You will declare it in Bicep, and see which mistakes the compiler catches. Two of three get through. {{exchange}} Last, the exchange itself. The pod sends its token to Entra ID, and gets back an access token for the storage account. No laptop plays Entra ID, so that part is read from Microsoft's documentation, and the lesson says exactly what Entra checks.
